articles.title: DOJ drags Army into court standoff with explosive warning for red state: report
articles.description: DOJ told a federal appeals court the Army can detonate Iowa’s unstable lead explosives without an EPA permit, The Washington Sun reported on Friday. The Army planned to destroy 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, the Sun wrote. After objections from Iowa and Illinois officials, it briefly delayed the plan, and environmental groups sued. The 8th Circuit paused the EPA’s emergency permit while it considers the case. In a Friday filing, a DOJ lawyer said an EPA rule lets the Army go ahead if it decides there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment,” according to the Sun. The Army isn’t a party to the suit. Army officials fear the aging explosive could go off by itself as it gets colder, the Sun reported, and the forecast shows temperatures falling Sunday and Monday nights. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said Monday was the last workable date before the drop. Iowa’s governor and many local communities said they heard about the plan only five days earlier, when the Army released maps showing lead dust could spread far from the plant, the paper wrote. The news of the planned detonation has triggered widespread fear throughout the region. Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau, who represents the plaintiffs, called the rule a last resort for cases with no other option. He asked the Army not to use it to avoid the transparency and protections people were demanding, the Sun reported. The Army, EPA, and Health and Human Services issued a joint statement Friday that didn’t mention the court order. It said officials had planned since March and were ready with strong safety measures, the Sun wrote. DOJ said it would respond to plaintiffs' emergency motion for a stay before Monday, the Sun reported.

articles.title: How Mamdani Plans to Finally Close New York’s Most Notorious Prison
articles.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s first year in office has been defined by solving small problems. By focusing on the local issues his city’s residents, in some cases, literally trip over every day, Mamdani is trying to show his administration as a perpetual motion machine. Now, the mayor’s propulsive pragmatism has come face-to-face with its biggest challenge yet: shuttering the jails at Rikers Island jail by 2032, a goal he announced on Friday. Unstoppable force, meet an immovable object. But the mayor’s unique ability to keep things moving—without ruffling too many feathers—may yet prove to be exactly what this long-delayed project needs. For decades, detainees at the notorious, century-old jail complex sandwiched between the Bronx and Queens have been subject to neglect, violence, and chaos. The carceral hazards are only compounded by the environmental ones. Custody is nearly four times longer than the national average, and assaults on both detainees and correctional staff occur at eight times the rate of similar jails, according to City Hall. Nine detainees have died so far this year. The island is not only literally toxic, but politically, too. Very little progress has been made since former New York City Mayor Bill DeBlasio first kicked the can down the road to closing Rikers by 2027. Under former New York City Mayor Eric Adams, Mamdani’s direct predecessor, City Hall not only consistently neglected the legally mandated deadline to close the facility, but even exacerbated the city’s incarceration problems. When Adams took office, about 5,400 people were in jail citywide; by the time he left office, more than 7,400 people were incarcerated, an increase of about 37 percent, according to the Data Collaborative for Justice. In a briefing Thursday night, City Hall outlined a suite of new investments and initiatives totaling more than $300 million, including: $67.5 million to demolish the facilities on Rikers; $50 million toward educational, vocational, and therapeutic programming; $30 million toward reducing the jail population in the FY27, and $76 million annually; and $4.5 million toward the planning process for the future use of Rikers Island as a site for renewable energy and resiliency infrastructure. City Hall’s full strategy can be found here. The new blueprint involves construction of four borough-based detention facilities by 2032, and reducing the population from 6,600 to 4,160 people. The plan also includes funding for an additional 246 hospital-based therapeutic beds in 2028, to bring the city’s total to more than 300. The Mamdani administration has already made some serious progress on its goals. In June, the Department of Correction (DOC) shuttered the North Infirmary Command, a vacant jail that opened on Rikers Island in 1932, and the city opened a therapeutic housing unit with more than 100 beds at NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue. Already, the disparate levels of government seem to be aligning. City Council Member Sandy Nurse is already drafting new legislation that would change the legally mandated closure date from 2027 to 2032, signalling that the City Council and City Hall are on the same page about the overall timeline. With the plans to demolish and rebuild facilities already underway, Mamdani’s administration is left with the daunting task of reducing the number of detainees in New York City’s jails. New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch has previously opposed criminal justice reforms, and Governor Kathy Hochul hasn’t always been the biggest fan of them, either. In order to reduce the city jails’ population without jeopardizing his fragile coalition of powerful actors across the state, Mamdani will have to do what he does best: solve small problems. In a prerecorded video released by City Hall, Mamdani and DOC Commissioner Stanley Richards discussed the city’s plans to address the delay in processing criminal cases, which keeps thousands of pretrial inmates incarcerated for months. “We’ll work across city agencies to speed up the exchange of evidence, and address court backlogs,” the mayor said. “We do not want any New Yorker to spend a day longer in detention than necessary.” “Evidence shows that unnecessary pretrial detention can increase the likelihood of conviction, job loss, and ultimately, re-arrest in the future, while case delay harms victims calling for justice,” Richards said, looking over the jail complex where he was once detained for roughly two-and-a-half years. He is the first formerly incarcerated person to run the agency. At first glance, City Hall’s ability to speed up criminal cases seems limited. New York City’s courts are funded by the state, and New York State has some of the strictest discovery processing laws in the country. But Mamdani’s administration is focused solely on what it can control: city agencies. City Hall plans to establish an Interagency Case Delay Task Force, alongside the Office of Court Administration, the city’s district attorneys, and the defense bar to develop their own slate of solutions. Speaking at a briefing Thursday, the city’s inaugural “close Rikers” czar Dana Kaplan said that the plan was more likely to succeed because it had been developed in conjunction with many of these key players in the court. City Hall also plans to accelerate the processing, sharing, and review of discovery. By improving the lines of communication between agencies such as the New York Police Department, Fire Department, and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, City Hall can address case delay while steering clear of tense policy disputes. Speaking to The New Republic earlier this week, Mamdani emphasized that City Hall’s “focus right now is looking at what we can unlock in the additional funding that we can provide.” Through this small-problem approach, the Mamdani administration can keep its momentum without leaning too much on its allies in Albany and the NYPD. There are those who will see the mayor’s budding alignment with the NYPD as a politically sensible approach to problem solving, and many others who will view it as a sort of betrayal of the activists who helped fuel the rise of the city’s first democratic socialist mayor. Clearly, dynamics have shifted. Mamdani previously touted the phrase “No New Jails.” Now, he’s planning to build four of them. But finally closing Rikers Island after decades may be exactly the kind of unifying issue that Mamdani is becoming known for. While the mayor’s loftier campaign promises, such as free buses and city-run grocery stores, have yet to materialize, his plan to close Rikers Islands already appears to be supported by a more unified political will. Whether City Hall is able to carry this long-delayed project across the finish line stands to be the ultimate test thus far of Mamdani’s perpetual motion machine, and whether it has enough power to pull everyone else along with it.

articles.title: Fiona and Harambe died 10 years apart at the same zoo. Both cases involved children.
articles.description: The death of Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo, was a tragedy — but it wasn’t the first to unfold at the zoo. In 2016, Harambe, an endangered Western Lowland gorilla, was fatally shot after he started dragging a little boy who had slipped into his enclosure. In a statement, the Cincinnati Zoo said that the child "climbed through a public barrier at Gorilla World and dropped fifteen feet into the exhibit's moat." When the zoo’s staff and Cincinnati Fire Department responded to the scene, Harambe “was violently dragging and throwing the child.” Minutes later, the Cincinnati Zoo’s Dangerous Animal Response Team — which includes full-time zookeepers, veterinarians, maintenance and security staff members — “made the difficult decision to put the gorilla down to save the child.” “We are heartbroken about losing Harambe, but a child’s life was in danger and a quick decision had to be made,” Thane Maynard, who was the Cincinnati Zoo’s director at the time, said at the time. “Our first response was to call the gorillas out of the exhibit. The two females complied, but Harambe did not." Maynard later defended the decision amid an outcry from wildlife conservationists who argued that the 17-year-old gorilla should have been tranquilized rather than killed. “The idea of waiting and shooting it with a hypodermic was not a good idea,” Maynard said at a press conference two days after the incident. “The risk was due to the power of that animal." After Harambe's death, the zoo reopened its gorilla exhibit with a higher, reinforced barrier. The death of Harambe was the biggest tragedy to rock the Cincinnati Zoo until Thursday, when zoo officials announced that its famed 9-year-old hippo Fiona had died after swallowing a knit cap that slipped into her enclosure. "It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said in a statement. What happened to Fiona? Michelle Curley, a zoo spokesperson, told reporters that Fiona ingested the knit hat on Nov. 8 after it was tossed in the air by a child and flung by a ceiling fan through a 1-foot opening above the viewing windows of her enclosure. "We probably couldn't make that happen again if we tried," Curley said. "It was clearly an accident." The zoo's animal care team spent days trying to help Fiona pass the obstruction, even using a vibration plate borrowed from a horse farm to help shake it through her digestive tract. An ultrasound showed bunching in Fiona's intestines; a colonoscopy with a 9-foot scope didn't help, nor did a "giant" enema. According to veterinarians, surgery wasn't an option for a full-grown Nile hippopotamus. "They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don't regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does," Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University's College of Veterinary Medicine, told the Associated Press. "Those multiple chambers, tissue folds, fluid and digesting food easily 'hide' the hat, making removal with an endoscope from the stomach chambers very difficult." In the days that followed, Fiona's appetite started to wane. "Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said. "We are in shock at the moment. We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore." Maynard, now the zoo’s executive chairman, added: "I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And she will be remembered and beloved many years from now." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/fiona-the-hippos-tragic-death-at-the-cincinnati-zoo-came-10-years-after-harambe-the-gorillas-controversial-killing-162041500.html

articles.title: Bari Weiss’s Reign at CBS Drives Dozens More Staffers to Leave
articles.description: A wave of buyouts at CBS News has resulted in dozens of departures from every corner of the company. CBS News staff were given until Wednesday to accept a buyout from Skydance, the company owned by David Ellison, the son of Trump’s good friend Larry Ellison. One CBS News staffer told Status the departures were an “extinction-level event.” The buyouts have reportedly decimated the foreign news desk: Puck News’s Dylan Byers reported that one-third of the organization’s London office took buyouts. The buyouts also saw departures from 60 Minutes, the Evening News, and the network’s bureau in Washington. Mounting reports suggest that CBS News’s foreign coverage has struggled under the leadership of Bari Weiss, who has repeatedly placed her own pro-Israel politics at the center of the organization’s reporting. Last month, Weiss reportedly became “very, very hands-on” with a story about violent Israeli settlers driving Palestinians out of the West Bank. It was so bad that 60 Minutes veteran Lesley Stahl even threatened to quit. Around the same time, Weiss’s handpicked foreign editor Shayndi Raice reportedly blocked CBS correspondent Holly Williams from reporting the death toll in Gaza. Speaking to staff Wednesday morning, Raice appeared emotional, perhaps about the toll the buyouts would take on her own desk, Status reported. Since Weiss’s installation, there has been a talent exodus from the news outlet, including Anderson Cooper, longtime 60 Minutes executive producer Bill Owens, CBS News producer Mary Walsh, CBS Evening News producer Alicia Hastey, and 60 Minutes host Sharyn Alfonsi.

articles.title: Child casualties in Ukraine reach highest level in almost four years – UNICEF
articles.description: *As families prepare to face winter, verified attacks on energy infrastructure have reached unprecedented levels since the start of the full-scale war* **KYIV, 20 November 2026** – At least 1,144 children have been killed or injured in Ukraine in the first ten months of 2026, a higher number of verified child casualties than in any of the past three years. According to the Human Rights Monitoring Mission for Ukraine (HRMMU), at least 114 children have been killed and 1,030 injured between January and October this year. That is an average of more than three children killed or injured every single day. Overnight, large-scale attacks were reported in Kyiv and several other parts of the country, killing and injuring civilians as well as damaging critical infrastructure. Last month alone, at least 146 children were killed or injured across Ukraine, a 150 per cent increase when compared to the same period last year. These latest figures reflect an alarming escalation in violence affecting children in Ukraine. Attacks involving missiles and armed drones continue to put children and families at risk in their homes, schools, and communities, including far from the frontline. With two months remaining in the year, the number of children killed in Ukraine in 2026 has already exceeded the total for 2025 by more than 20 per cent, while the number of children injured has risen by almost 60 per cent. “Children have been paying an unacceptable price for this war for too long. Every child killed is a life and future lost, and every child injured may face lasting physical and psychological consequences. Children must be protected, wherever they are,” said UNICEF Representative in Ukraine, Anne-Claire Dufay. “Today is World Children’s Day, when we should be celebrating children’s rights. But in Ukraine they continue to live in fear in their homes, neighborhoods, and places where they should feel safe.” Deadly attacks against civilians have indeed continued into this month. On 2 November, a strike on a school compound in Southeastern Ukraine, including an underground shelter where humanitarian assistance was being distributed, reportedly killed 72 people, with four others still missing. On 13 November, a 17-year-old boy was reportedly killed and eight other children injured in attacks on Zaporizhzhia city, underscoring the continued threat to children’s lives and safety. In addition, verified attacks on energy infrastructure in 2026 are at their highest level since the start of the full-scale war, with 78 per cent more attacks already verified than in all of 2025. Scheduled outages are now in force across most regions, lasting between 4 and 18 hours, with power cuts exceeding 12 hours in early November, as heating and power plants continue to be heavily damaged. When power is cut, water supplies to homes, schools, and health facilities can also be disrupted, leaving children without safe water for drinking and hygiene and increasing the risk of disease. Last winter, nearly two million children were left without heat, electricity, and water as temperatures fell below minus 20°C. UNICEF is supporting district energy projects to maintain heating for around three million people in the hardest-hit municipalities. With partners, UNICEF is installing alternative power sources in health facilities to keep essential maternal and child health services running, and solar power at critical water supply sites serving around 2.5 million people. With the Ministry of Social Policy, UNICEF is also providing winter cash assistance to more than 100,000 households in frontline regions. UNICEF and partners are also repairing damaged education facilities, rehabilitating school shelters, and providing learning, mental health, and psychosocial support to children, young people, and families. Despite all efforts, too many children in Ukraine continue to be at the sharp end of unrelenting war. UNICEF calls for the protection of civilians, including children, and the infrastructure they depend on, including energy, heating, and water systems, in accordance with international humanitarian law. Safe and unimpeded humanitarian access across Ukraine, including occupied territories, remains critical.
